chapterMetadata.title: Laws of Motion
chapterMetadata.subject: Science (Physics)
learningObjectives: Understand Newton's three laws of motion and their applications
Relate force, mass, and acceleration using the equation F = ma
Distinguish between balanced and unbalanced forces
Recognize real-life examples of inertia, momentum, and action-reaction

prerequisites: Knowledge of basic physical quantities like force, mass, and velocity
Familiarity with the concept of motion from previous classes

sections.title: 1.1 Newton's First Law of Motion
sections.summary: An object remains in a state of rest or uniform motion unless acted upon by an external force.

keyConcepts.name: Inertia
keyConcepts.description: The tendency of an object to resist a change in its state of motion.
properties: Different types: inertia of rest, inertia of motion, inertia of direction

sections.title: 1.2 Newton's Second Law of Motion
sections.summary: The acceleration of an object is directly proportional to the net force acting on it and inversely proportional to its mass.

keyConcepts.name: Force Equation
keyConcepts.description: F = ma (Force equals mass times acceleration).
properties: Basis for unit of force: Newton (N)

sections.title: 1.3 Newton's Third Law of Motion
sections.summary: For every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction.

keyConcepts.name: Action-Reaction Pairs
keyConcepts.description: Forces that always exist in pairs acting on different bodies.

examples.equation: A football remains at rest until kicked.
examples.explanation: Illustrates Newton’s First Law (inertia of rest).

examples.equation: A heavier object requires more force to accelerate.
Rocket propulsion works by expelling gases backward.

exercises: State Newton’s First Law with an example.
Calculate the force needed to accelerate a 5 kg mass at 2 m/s².
Identify the action-reaction pair when a person jumps off a boat.

vocabulary.definition: Tendency of a body to resist changes in motion.
Product of mass and velocity (p = mv).
A push or pull that changes or tends to change the state of motion of an object.

misconceptions: Many think a force is needed to keep an object moving, but in absence of friction, no force is required.
Some students confuse action-reaction forces as acting on the same object, but they act on different objects.
applications: Seat belts in cars work due to inertia (First Law).
Sports like football, cricket, and baseball demonstrate Newton's Second Law.
Rocket launching is an application of Newton's Third Law.
heritage: Sir Isaac Newton formulated the three laws of motion in 1687 in his work Principia Mathematica.
Ancient Indian texts like Vaisheshika Sutra also discussed early concepts of motion.
